lines.text: A hundred miles out at sea. No towers, no signal. And yet, you're streaming video. How?
Your phone normally talks to a cell tower. But a tower only reaches a few dozen kilometers. Past the coast, there's nothing.
Old satellite internet used satellites thirty-six thousand kilometers up. So far away that every message takes over half a second to go there and back.
Starlink flies much lower, about five hundred and fifty kilometers up. So the trip takes just a few hundredths of a second.
But low satellites race across the sky, circling Earth in about an hour and a half. So Starlink uses thousands of them, a whole swarm.
On the ship sits a flat dish. It doesn't swing around to chase satellites. Inside, hundreds of tiny antennas steer the beam electronically, hopping from one satellite to the next.
Near land, the satellite beams your data straight down to a ground station, wired into the internet.
But in the middle of the ocean, there's no ground station below. So the satellites pass your data to each other, with lasers, across space.
Hop, hop, hop, until a satellite is above a station on land. Then it drops down, and you're online.
And once you're online, even at sea, Orbi Transfer works too. No login, files locked before they leave.
